questions.question: Q: Name the most common bacterial cause of food poisoning in the UK.

points.text: Campylobacter, often found in undercooked poultry.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between food poisoning by infection and by intoxication?

points.text: Infection: caused by eating food containing live bacteria that multiply in the gut. Intoxication: caused by eating food containing toxins already produced by bacteria before the food is eaten.

questions.question: Q: Which bacterium produces toxins in food and is carried on human skin?

points.text: Staphylococcus aureus. It is carried on skin and in nasal passages, and can transfer to food through poor hand hygiene.

questions.question: Q: What is cross-contamination and why is it dangerous?

points.text: Cross-contamination is the transfer of harmful bacteria from one food (usually raw meat/poultry) to ready-to-eat food. It is the most common cause of food poisoning.

questions.question: Q: Name two sources of E. coli O157 and a serious complication it can cause.

points.text: Sources: undercooked minced beef and unpasteurised milk. Complication: haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), which can cause kidney failure.

questions.question: Q: Why is Clostridium perfringens particularly difficult to eliminate through cooking?

points.text: It forms heat-resistant spores that can survive normal cooking temperatures. If food is then left at room temperature, the spores germinate and the bacteria multiply rapidly.

questions.question: Q: Give three ways to prevent cross-contamination.

points.text: Use separate chopping boards for raw and cooked food, wash hands thoroughly after handling raw meat, store raw meat below ready-to-eat food in the fridge, and clean and disinfect surfaces between tasks (any three).

questions.question: Q: What is norovirus and how is it commonly spread?

points.text: Norovirus is a virus (the 'winter vomiting bug') spread through contaminated food, water, surfaces, or poor personal hygiene, especially by food handlers who are ill.
